title: Price each trade using only information known then
prompt: A trading system stores versioned product quotes. Price every trade with the single winning quote that was both effective and published by the trade instant. Return trade_id, sku, quoted_price, gross_amount, price_status, ordered by trade_id ascending. Retain trades with no eligible quote and distinguish them from explicit price suspensions.
businessRules: All TIMESTAMP values are timezone-naive UTC. A quote is eligible only for the same sku and when effective_at <= traded_at AND published_at <= traded_at; both boundaries are inclusive.
Among eligible quotes, choose the greatest effective_at, then greatest published_at, then greatest price_id. A newer publication of an older effective quote must not outrank a newer effective quote.
A winning NULL unit_price means SUSPENDED. Do not fall back to an older non-NULL quote. No eligible quote means NO_PRICE. Otherwise price_status is PRICED, including a zero quote.
quoted_price is the winning unit_price; gross_amount is quantity * quoted_price. Both amounts are NULL for SUSPENDED or NO_PRICE.
Trade IDs and price IDs are unique and non-null. sku and all timestamps are non-null; quantity is a positive integer. Only unit_price may be NULL. Return exactly one row per trade.

tables.name: s01_trades
tables.description: Trades requiring the price known at the trade instant.

tables.name: s01_prices
tables.description: Versioned quotes; effective time and publication time are separate.

columns.name: price_id
columns.description: Unique non-null quote identifier, also the final tie-breaker

columns.name: effective_at
columns.description: When this quote becomes economically effective

columns.name: unit_price
columns.description: NULL means explicitly suspended; zero is a valid price

starterSql:
-- Find eligible quotes, rank them separately for each trade, and retain rank 1.
SELECT trade_id, sku, traded_at, quantity
FROM s01_trades
ORDER BY trade_id;
solutionSql:
WITH ranked_quotes AS (
    SELECT t.trade_id, t.sku, t.quantity, p.price_id, p.unit_price,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY t.trade_id
               ORDER BY p.effective_at DESC NULLS LAST,
                        p.published_at DESC NULLS LAST,
                        p.price_id DESC NULLS LAST
           ) AS quote_rank
    FROM s01_trades AS t
    LEFT JOIN s01_prices AS p
      ON p.sku = t.sku
     AND p.effective_at <= t.traded_at
     AND p.published_at <= t.traded_at
)
SELECT trade_id, sku, unit_price AS quoted_price,
       quantity * unit_price AS gross_amount,
       CASE WHEN price_id IS NULL THEN 'NO_PRICE'
            WHEN unit_price IS NULL THEN 'SUSPENDED'
            ELSE 'PRICED' END AS price_status
FROM ranked_quotes
WHERE quote_rank = 1
ORDER BY trade_id;
explanation: The left join limits candidates using both clocks before ranking. Its unmatched row is intentional: ROW_NUMBER still emits one row for a trade with no eligible quote.

Ranking begins with effective_at, so a late revision of an older effective quote cannot displace a newer effective quote. published_at and price_id make the choice deterministic within that effective time.
Check price_id for the absence of a match; checking only unit_price would collapse NO_PRICE and SUSPENDED. Do not filter NULL prices before ranking.

Trade 103 still uses quote 4 because quote 5 is not published until noon. At noon, quote 6 wins by effective time and suspends pricing. Trade 107 uses quote 11 even though older-effective quote 10 is published later.
hints: First write the two inequalities that make a quote eligible for one trade. Keep unmatched trades with a LEFT JOIN.
Within each trade, rank eligible rows by effective time, publication time, and price ID, all descending. Apply eligibility before ranking.
After selecting rank 1, use the quote identifier to distinguish a missing match from a matched quote whose price is NULL. Zero needs no special treatment.
pitfalls: Looking only at effective_at leaks quotes published after the trade.
Picking the latest published quote can incorrectly choose an older effective price.
Filtering unit_price IS NOT NULL silently undoes suspensions.
Using an INNER JOIN drops trades without prices; omitting the ID tie-breaker makes ties nondeterministic.

title: Find every uncovered interval after merging overlaps
prompt: Audit service coverage during the fixed UTC interval [2026-04-01 00:00:00, 2026-04-01 12:00:00). Return every maximal uncovered interval for every registered resource. Output resource_id, gap_start, gap_end, gap_minutes, ordered by resource_id ascending and gap_start ascending. Return gap_start and gap_end as VARCHAR timestamp strings; omit resources with complete coverage.
businessRules: All timestamps are timezone-naive UTC and minute-aligned. Every interval is half-open: starts_at is included and ends_at is excluded.
Ignore rows with NULL starts_at, with a non-NULL ends_at <= starts_at, or with resource_id absent from s02_resources. A NULL ends_at means indefinitely open coverage.
Clip valid coverage to the fixed reporting window. Intervals that only touch the reporting boundary contribute no coverage.
Merge overlapping and exactly touching coverage, including nested intervals and duplicate ranges. Emit positive-length maximal gaps only; gap_minutes is their integer duration.

Include a full-window gap for every registered resource with no coverage. Registered resource IDs and coverage IDs are unique and non-null; coverage resource_id is non-null. Do not assume raw intervals are ordered.

tables.name: s02_resources
tables.description: Every resource that must be audited, including resources with no valid coverage.

tables.name: s02_coverage
tables.description: Raw half-open coverage intervals; malformed rows must be ignored.

columns.name: starts_at
columns.description: UTC inclusive start; NULL means invalid

columns.name: ends_at
columns.description: UTC exclusive end; NULL means open-ended

starterSql:
-- Normalize and clip coverage before finding islands and their complement.
SELECT resource_id, coverage_id, starts_at, ends_at
FROM s02_coverage
ORDER BY resource_id, starts_at, coverage_id;
solutionSql:
WITH params AS (
    SELECT TIMESTAMP '2026-04-01 00:00:00' AS window_start,
           TIMESTAMP '2026-04-01 12:00:00' AS window_end
), clipped AS (
    SELECT c.coverage_id, c.resource_id,
           GREATEST(c.starts_at, p.window_start) AS starts_at,
           LEAST(COALESCE(c.ends_at, p.window_end), p.window_end) AS ends_at
    FROM s02_coverage AS c
    JOIN s02_resources AS r ON r.resource_id = c.resource_id
    CROSS JOIN params AS p
    WHERE c.starts_at IS NOT NULL
      AND (c.ends_at IS NULL OR c.ends_at > c.starts_at)
      AND c.starts_at < p.window_end
      AND COALESCE(c.ends_at, p.window_end) > p.window_start
), prior_reach AS (
    SELECT *,
           MAX(ends_at) OVER (
               PARTITION BY resource_id
               ORDER BY starts_at, ends_at, coverage_id
               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING
           ) AS prior_end
    FROM clipped
), marked AS (
    SELECT *, CASE WHEN prior_end IS NULL OR starts_at > prior_end
                   THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS starts_island
    FROM prior_reach
), numbered AS (
    SELECT *, SUM(starts_island) OVER (
        PARTITION BY resource_id ORDER BY starts_at, ends_at, coverage_id
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS island_id
    FROM marked
), islands AS (
    SELECT resource_id, MIN(starts_at) AS starts_at, MAX(ends_at) AS ends_at
    FROM numbered
    GROUP BY resource_id, island_id
), bounded AS (
    SELECT resource_id, starts_at, ends_at FROM islands
    UNION ALL
    SELECT r.resource_id, p.window_start, p.window_start
    FROM s02_resources AS r CROSS JOIN params AS p
    UNION ALL
    SELECT r.resource_id, p.window_end, p.window_end
    FROM s02_resources AS r CROSS JOIN params AS p
), gaps AS (
    SELECT resource_id, ends_at AS gap_start,
           LEAD(starts_at) OVER (
               PARTITION BY resource_id ORDER BY starts_at, ends_at
           ) AS gap_end
    FROM bounded
)
SELECT resource_id, CAST(gap_start AS VARCHAR) AS gap_start,
       CAST(gap_end AS VARCHAR) AS gap_end,
       DATE_DIFF('minute', gap_start, gap_end) AS gap_minutes
FROM gaps
WHERE gap_end > gap_start
ORDER BY resource_id, gap_start;
explanation: Clip only valid intersecting intervals. This makes open-ended coverage finite and removes intervals with zero contribution to the report.

The prior running MAX(ends_at), excluding the current row, records the furthest coverage reached by any earlier interval. A new island begins only when starts_at is strictly beyond that reach; equality keeps touching intervals together.
Aggregate each island to one start and end. Add zero-length sentinels at both report boundaries for every registered resource, then use LEAD to find the space between merged coverage ranges.
R1 is covered continuously from midnight to 08:00 despite nested rows, then from 10:00 to 11:00. R2 is covered from 02:00 onward. R3 has no valid intersecting coverage. R4 is fully covered.
hints: First reject invalid rows and clip the remaining half-open intervals to the reporting window.
An immediately previous end is not enough when intervals nest. Compare each start with the maximum end of all earlier intervals, then number the islands.
After merging islands, add both window boundaries for every resource. The positive spaces between consecutive ranges are the maximal gaps, including for resources with no ranges.
pitfalls: Using LAG(ends_at) instead of the prior running maximum invents gaps inside a longer enclosing interval.
Treating touching intervals as disconnected or using inclusive end boundaries creates zero-length or false gaps.
Dropping NULL ends loses open-ended coverage; retaining NULL starts invents coverage.
Starting from coverage rather than the resource registry loses resources with no valid intervals.

title: Compute mature anniversary-week retention without censoring bias
prompt: Measure session retention as of the exclusive UTC cutoff 2026-06-22 00:00:00. Group users into Monday-start signup cohorts, but measure weeks 0, 1, and 2 from each user's exact signup instant. Return cohort_week, week_number, eligible_users, retained_users, retention_pct, ordered by cohort_week ascending then week_number ascending. cohort_week must be a YYYY-MM-DD VARCHAR. Include all three week rows for every cohort with at least one signup before the cutoff, even if no user is yet eligible.
businessRules: All timestamps are timezone-naive UTC. Exclude users whose signup_at >= the cutoff. cohort_week is the Monday date of the week containing signup_at.
For week k in {0,1,2}, a user's window is [signup_at + 7*k days, signup_at + 7*(k+1) days). These are exact seven-day anniversary windows, not calendar-week buckets.
A user is eligible for week k only when the entire window has ended by the cutoff: window_end <= cutoff. Do not include partially observed windows in either count.

An eligible user is retained if at least one event has event_type exactly session and occurred_at within that user's half-open window. Count users once, regardless of duplicate events. Events at the cutoff, before signup, for unknown users, or with NULL user_id do not contribute.

eligible_users and retained_users are integer counts. retention_pct = 100 * retained_users / eligible_users, rounded to two decimal places; it is NULL when eligible_users is zero. All other counts are zero, not NULL, for zero-eligible rows.
user_id is unique and non-null in s03_users; signup_at is non-null. event_id is unique and non-null; occurred_at and event_type are non-null. Only event user_id may be NULL.

tables.name: s03_users
tables.description: Signup instants determine anniversary-week windows; users at or after the cutoff are excluded.

tables.name: s03_events
tables.description: Activity stream may include duplicates, non-session events, and unmatched user IDs.

columns.name: user_id
columns.description: May be NULL or absent from the user table

columns.name: event_type
columns.description: Only the exact value session qualifies

starterSql:
-- Scaffold three windows per admitted user before aggregating cohort metrics.
WITH weeks(week_number) AS (VALUES (0), (1), (2))
SELECT u.user_id, u.signup_at, w.week_number
FROM s03_users AS u CROSS JOIN weeks AS w
WHERE u.signup_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-06-22 00:00:00'
ORDER BY u.user_id, w.week_number;
solutionSql:
WITH params AS (
    SELECT TIMESTAMP '2026-06-22 00:00:00' AS cutoff
), weeks(week_number) AS (
    VALUES (0), (1), (2)
), user_windows AS (
    SELECT u.user_id,
           CAST(DATE_TRUNC('week', u.signup_at) AS DATE) AS cohort_week,
           w.week_number, p.cutoff,
           u.signup_at + (7 * w.week_number) * INTERVAL '1 day' AS window_start,
           u.signup_at + (7 * (w.week_number + 1)) * INTERVAL '1 day' AS window_end
    FROM s03_users AS u
    CROSS JOIN weeks AS w
    CROSS JOIN params AS p
    WHERE u.signup_at < p.cutoff
), flags AS (
    SELECT uw.*,
           CASE WHEN uw.window_end <= uw.cutoff THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS eligible,
           CASE WHEN uw.window_end <= uw.cutoff AND EXISTS (
               SELECT 1
               FROM s03_events AS e
               WHERE e.user_id = uw.user_id
                 AND e.event_type = 'session'
                 AND e.occurred_at >= uw.window_start
                 AND e.occurred_at < uw.window_end
                 AND e.occurred_at < uw.cutoff
           ) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS retained
    FROM user_windows AS uw
)
SELECT CAST(cohort_week AS VARCHAR) AS cohort_week, week_number,
       SUM(eligible) AS eligible_users,
       SUM(retained) AS retained_users,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(retained) / NULLIF(SUM(eligible), 0), 2) AS retention_pct
FROM flags
GROUP BY cohort_week, week_number
ORDER BY cohort_week, week_number;
explanation: Cross join admitted users with weeks 0, 1, and 2. Keeping those rows before the eligibility check ensures every observed cohort has all requested week rows.
Eligibility depends on each user's exact window end. This avoids right-censoring bias: users who have not had a full opportunity to return are removed from both the numerator and denominator.
EXISTS reduces any number of qualifying events to one retained flag. Half-open windows put a boundary event into exactly one anniversary week.

For cohort 2026-06-01, both users are eligible for weeks 0 and 1, but only user 1 is eligible for week 2. This yields 50%, 100%, and 100%. The June 15 cohort has one mature week-0 user with no qualifying session; later weeks have no eligible users.
hints: Build the cohort label separately from the per-user anniversary windows. Generate weeks 0, 1, and 2 even if activity is absent.
Mark eligibility using window_end <= cutoff. Then test for at least one session inside each eligible half-open window; an EXISTS test avoids counting events as users.
Aggregate the eligibility and retained flags by cohort and week. Divide by eligible users, return NULL for a zero denominator, and preserve the zero-eligible rows.
pitfalls: Using the full cohort size as every denominator penalizes users whose retention windows are incomplete.
Using calendar-week differences misclassifies events for users who signed up later in the week or later in the day.
Counting event rows inflates retention when a user has multiple sessions.
Filtering to eligible rows or joining only observed events drops requested zero-eligible or zero-retained rows.
Using BETWEEN includes the upper boundary and can count the same event in two windows.

title: Find the first inventory deficit episode
prompt: An inventory team wants the first out-of-stock deficit episode for every SKU/warehouse pair before the report cutoff, 2026-01-03 00:00:00 UTC. Starting from its nonnegative snapshot quantity, apply eligible inventory movements and report the start, recovery, and deepest negative balance of only the first episode. Return sku, warehouse, breach_start_utc, recovered_at_utc, lowest_balance in that order. Format the two timestamps as VARCHAR; leave recovered_at_utc NULL if the first episode is still open at cutoff. Omit pairs that never become negative. Sort by sku, then warehouse, ascending.
businessRules: Each opening snapshot already includes every movement at or before snapshot_at. Include movements strictly after that pair's snapshot and strictly before 2026-01-03 00:00:00 UTC.
Every timestamp is a timezone-naive TIMESTAMP interpreted as UTC. Do not convert timezones or truncate timestamps to dates.
For one SKU/warehouse, all movements with exactly the same timestamp are atomic: sum their deltas before evaluating the resulting balance. movement_id is an identifier, not a business ordering rule.

An episode begins when the post-timestamp balance is strictly negative. A balance of zero or greater ends it. Nonnegative opening quantities guarantee the first negative timestamp is the first episode's start.
The first episode's lowest_balance uses states from its start up to, but not including, its recovery timestamp. Later deficit episodes must not affect the answer.
Only SKU/warehouse pairs present in inv04_openings are in scope. All input key, quantity, and timestamp columns are non-NULL; a missing recovery is represented by SQL NULL.

tables.name: inv04_openings
tables.description: One nonnegative balance snapshot per SKU/warehouse. Snapshot-time movements are already included.

tables.name: inv04_movements
tables.description: Signed unit movements; duplicate timestamps represent one atomic business instant.

starterSql:
-- Build timestamp-level deltas, then running balances and the first episode.
SELECT sku, warehouse,
       CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS breach_start_utc,
       CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS recovered_at_utc,
       CAST(NULL AS BIGINT) AS lowest_balance
FROM inv04_openings
WHERE FALSE
ORDER BY sku, warehouse;
solutionSql:
WITH timestamp_deltas AS (
  SELECT m.sku, m.warehouse, m.occurred_at,
         o.opening_qty, SUM(m.qty_delta) AS qty_delta
  FROM inv04_movements AS m
  JOIN inv04_openings AS o
    ON o.sku = m.sku AND o.warehouse = m.warehouse
  WHERE m.occurred_at > o.snapshot_at
    AND m.occurred_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-01-03 00:00:00'
  GROUP BY m.sku, m.warehouse, m.occurred_at, o.opening_qty
), balances AS (
  SELECT sku, warehouse, occurred_at,
         opening_qty + SUM(qty_delta) OVER (
           PARTITION BY sku, warehouse
           ORDER BY occurred_at
           ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
         ) AS balance
  FROM timestamp_deltas
), first_breach AS (
  SELECT sku, warehouse, MIN(occurred_at) AS breach_at
  FROM balances
  WHERE balance < 0
  GROUP BY sku, warehouse
), first_recovery AS (
  SELECT f.sku, f.warehouse, f.breach_at,
         MIN(b.occurred_at) AS recovered_at
  FROM first_breach AS f
  LEFT JOIN balances AS b
    ON b.sku = f.sku AND b.warehouse = f.warehouse
   AND b.occurred_at > f.breach_at
   AND b.balance >= 0
  GROUP BY f.sku, f.warehouse, f.breach_at
)
SELECT r.sku, r.warehouse,
       CAST(r.breach_at AS VARCHAR) AS breach_start_utc,
       CAST(r.recovered_at AS VARCHAR) AS recovered_at_utc,
       MIN(b.balance) AS lowest_balance
FROM first_recovery AS r
JOIN balances AS b
  ON b.sku = r.sku AND b.warehouse = r.warehouse
 AND b.occurred_at >= r.breach_at
 AND (r.recovered_at IS NULL OR b.occurred_at < r.recovered_at)
GROUP BY r.sku, r.warehouse, r.breach_at, r.recovered_at
ORDER BY r.sku, r.warehouse;
explanation: Filter the ledger using each pair's snapshot and the exclusive report cutoff, then collapse same-timestamp movements before computing a running SUM.
Add opening_qty to the cumulative delta. Because every opening is nonnegative, the earliest negative state is the first breach without needing to label all later episodes.
For each first breach, find the first later nonnegative state. LEFT JOIN preserves episodes without a recovery.

starterSql:
-- Normalize keys, number duplicate occurrences per source, then align slots.
SELECT CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS normalized_ref,
       CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS currency,
       CAST(NULL AS BIGINT) AS amount_cents,
       CAST(NULL AS BIGINT) AS occurrence_no,
       CAST(NULL AS BIGINT) AS erp_row_id,
       CAST(NULL AS BIGINT) AS gateway_row_id,
       CAST(NULL AS BIGINT) AS bank_row_id,
       CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS missing_sources
WHERE FALSE;
solutionSql:
WITH normalized AS (
  SELECT row_id, source,
         NULLIF(UPPER(TRIM(external_ref)), '') AS normalized_ref,
         UPPER(TRIM(currency)) AS currency,
         amount_cents
  FROM rec05_lines
), numbered AS (
  SELECT *,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY source, normalized_ref, currency, amount_cents
           ORDER BY row_id
         ) AS occurrence_no
  FROM normalized
), aligned AS (
  SELECT normalized_ref, currency, amount_cents, occurrence_no,
         MAX(CASE WHEN source = 'erp' THEN row_id END) AS erp_row_id,
         MAX(CASE WHEN source = 'gateway' THEN row_id END) AS gateway_row_id,
         MAX(CASE WHEN source = 'bank' THEN row_id END) AS bank_row_id
  FROM numbered
  GROUP BY normalized_ref, currency, amount_cents, occurrence_no
)
SELECT normalized_ref, currency, amount_cents, occurrence_no,
       erp_row_id, gateway_row_id, bank_row_id,
       CONCAT_WS(',',
         CASE WHEN erp_row_id IS NULL THEN 'erp' END,
         CASE WHEN gateway_row_id IS NULL THEN 'gateway' END,
         CASE WHEN bank_row_id IS NULL THEN 'bank' END
       ) AS missing_sources
FROM aligned
WHERE erp_row_id IS NULL OR gateway_row_id IS NULL OR bank_row_id IS NULL
ORDER BY normalized_ref ASC NULLS FIRST,
         currency ASC, amount_cents ASC, occurrence_no ASC;

title: Attribution without stealing the conversion
prompt: A growth team uses a seven-day last-non-direct attribution model. Attribute every conversion to exactly one eligible touch, while retaining conversions with no match. Return conversion_id, attributed_channel, touch_id, hours_since_touch, ordered by conversion_id. Round elapsed hours to two decimal places.
businessRules: All timestamps are UTC. The eligibility window is [converted_at minus 7 days, converted_at], including both endpoints.
A touch matches only the same non-NULL user_id. Anonymous conversions must remain unattributed, even if anonymous touches exist.
If any eligible non-direct touch exists, select the latest non-direct touch. Otherwise choose the latest eligible direct touch.
Break equal touched_at timestamps by higher touch_id. A touch can be credited to multiple conversions; it is not consumed.
For no eligible touch, use attributed_channel = 'unattributed' and NULL for touch_id and hours_since_touch. Channel values are never NULL.

tables.name: a07_conversions
tables.description: One row per conversion; anonymous user IDs are NULL.

tables.name: a07_touches
tables.description: One row per touch. touch_id is unique and is the deterministic tie-breaker.

starterSql:
-- Rank eligible touches separately for each conversion.
SELECT * FROM a07_conversions ORDER BY conversion_id;
solutionSql:
WITH eligible AS (
  SELECT c.conversion_id, c.converted_at,
         t.touch_id, t.touched_at, t.channel,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY c.conversion_id
           ORDER BY CASE WHEN t.channel <> 'direct' THEN 0 ELSE 1 END,
                    t.touched_at DESC, t.touch_id DESC
         ) AS choice
  FROM a07_conversions c
  LEFT JOIN a07_touches t
    ON c.user_id = t.user_id
   AND t.touched_at >= c.converted_at - INTERVAL '7 days'
   AND t.touched_at <= c.converted_at
)
SELECT conversion_id,
       COALESCE(channel, 'unattributed') AS attributed_channel,
       touch_id,
       CAST(ROUND(DATE_DIFF('second', touched_at, converted_at) / 3600.0, 2)
            AS DECIMAL(12,2)) AS hours_since_touch
FROM eligible
WHERE choice = 1
ORDER BY conversion_id;
explanation: Build eligible touch candidates with time conditions inside the LEFT JOIN so a conversion with no candidates still survives.
Rank non-direct candidates before direct ones, then newest timestamp and highest touch ID. Partition by conversion_id, not user_id, because users can convert more than once.
Keeping choice = 1 yields exactly one row per conversion. Elapsed seconds divided by 3600 gives duration, rather than counting crossed clock-hour boundaries.
hints: Start with a LEFT JOIN from conversions. Put the eligibility window in ON, not WHERE.
The ordering must first prefer non-direct channels, then recency, then touch_id. Partition the ranking by conversion_id.
Use ROW_NUMBER(), keep rank 1, and compute DATE_DIFF('second', touched_at, converted_at) / 3600.0.
pitfalls: Taking the most recent touch blindly credits direct traffic for conversions 101 and 105.
Partitioning by user_id collapses multiple conversions into one row.
Using a null-safe user join incorrectly links anonymous people.
Moving touch filters into WHERE turns the LEFT JOIN into an effective inner join.

NULL user IDs do not identify the same person, so anonymous touch 9 cannot match.

title: Replay-safe CDC with tombstones
prompt: Build the next account snapshot from a stored snapshot and a replay-prone CDC batch, as of the ingestion cutoff 2026-01-11 00:00:00 UTC. Return account_id, last_seq, is_deleted, email, plan ordered by account_id. Keep tombstones in the result so later replays cannot resurrect deleted accounts.
businessRules: The existing snapshot has at most one row per account, including deleted accounts. account_id, source_seq and ingest_id are non-NULL; sequence numbers increase within an account.
Only delta rows ingested strictly before 2026-01-11 00:00:00 UTC are visible. Source sequence determines business order; arrival time does not.
For accounts already in the snapshot, ignore every delta with source_seq <= last_seq. Existing state wins ties with its watermark.

Among eligible deltas, greatest source_seq wins; for conflicting rows at the same source_seq, greatest ingest_id wins. Repeated identical rows sharing ingest_id are transport duplicates and are harmless.
operation is U (full replacement) or D (deletion). NULL in a U payload is a genuine replacement value, not 'keep the old value'.
A winning D row is retained with is_deleted = true and NULL email/plan, even if its payload is populated. A later-sequence U can recreate the account. Unchanged snapshot rows remain.

ingest_id is a nonnegative integer. Rows sharing ingest_id are identical transport copies; distinct conflicting records have different ingest IDs. The stored snapshot represents valid normalized state, with NULL payloads on tombstones.

tables.name: c08_snapshot
tables.description: Previously materialized state, including tombstones and their sequence watermark.

tables.name: c08_delta
tables.description: Full replacement records. Exact transport duplicates can repeat an ingest_id.

starterSql:
-- Compare each source sequence with the stored watermark before ranking.
SELECT * FROM c08_delta ORDER BY account_id, source_seq, ingest_id;
solutionSql:
WITH eligible_delta AS (
  SELECT d.*
  FROM c08_delta d
  LEFT JOIN c08_snapshot s ON d.account_id = s.account_id
  WHERE d.ingested_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-01-11 00:00:00'
    AND (s.account_id IS NULL OR d.source_seq > s.last_seq)
), candidates AS (
  SELECT account_id, last_seq, is_deleted, email, plan, -1 AS ingest_id
  FROM c08_snapshot
  UNION ALL
  SELECT account_id, source_seq AS last_seq, operation = 'D' AS is_deleted,
         email, plan, ingest_id
  FROM eligible_delta
), ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY last_seq DESC, ingest_id DESC
  ) AS choice
  FROM candidates
)
SELECT account_id, last_seq, is_deleted,
       CASE WHEN is_deleted THEN NULL ELSE email END AS email,
       CASE WHEN is_deleted THEN NULL ELSE plan END AS plan
FROM ranked
WHERE choice = 1
ORDER BY account_id;

Union surviving changes with stored rows and rank once per account by source sequence, then ingest ID. Rank U and D together; deleting tombstones early would let old upserts win.
Preserve the winning sequence even on a deletion. Clear deletion payload fields after ranking, but do not coalesce NULL fields for a winning upsert.
hints: The newest arrival is not necessarily the newest business event. Filter deltas against both the cutoff and each account's stored sequence.
Treat a deletion as a candidate state and rank it alongside upserts. Union snapshot rows with eligible candidates.
ROW_NUMBER() by account_id with last_seq DESC, ingest_id DESC identifies the winner; null the payload only when that winning row is deleted.
pitfalls: Dropping D records before ranking resurrects account 3 and account 5.
Joining only non-deleted snapshot rows loses account 4's watermark.

Using <= at the ingestion cutoff includes account 7 too early.

The only delta arrives after the cutoff, so the existing state stays intact.

title: Revenue when refunds multiply rows
prompt: A finance model overstates January revenue after joining order lines to refunds. Produce a fanout-safe customer summary for paid orders placed in January 2026. Return customer_id, paid_orders, gross_cents, recognized_refund_cents, net_cents ordered by customer_id. Keep every customer with at least one qualifying order, including zero-value orders.
businessRules: All timestamps are UTC. Include paid orders with ordered_at >= 2026-01-01 00:00:00 and < 2026-02-01 00:00:00; ignore cancelled or out-of-period orders.
Each line amount is already extended gross value, in non-negative integer cents. Sum every distinct line ID; equal amounts are not duplicates.
Only succeeded refunds count. All provided refunds are known as of the report run; do not impose a separate refund-date filter.
Cap recognized refunds at each order's gross amount, then aggregate to customer. Do not cap only after aggregating a customer's orders.
A paid order with no lines has gross 0 and still counts as one paid order. Missing refunds mean 0. An order's net amount cannot be negative.
Order, line, and refund IDs are unique within their respective tables. Refunds are attached to orders, not individual lines.
All IDs, customer IDs, statuses, timestamps, and amounts are non-NULL. Refund amounts are nonnegative integer cents.

solutionSql:

  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount_cents) AS gross_cents
  FROM r09_lines GROUP BY order_id
), refund_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount_cents) AS refund_cents
  FROM r09_refunds
  WHERE status = 'succeeded'
  GROUP BY order_id
), per_order AS (
  SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id,
         COALESCE(l.gross_cents, 0) AS gross_cents,
         LEAST(COALESCE(l.gross_cents, 0),
               COALESCE(r.refund_cents, 0)) AS recognized_refund_cents
  FROM r09_orders o
  LEFT JOIN line_totals l ON o.order_id = l.order_id
  LEFT JOIN refund_totals r ON o.order_id = r.order_id
  WHERE o.status = 'paid'
    AND o.ordered_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00'
    AND o.ordered_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-02-01 00:00:00'

       SUM(gross_cents) AS gross_cents,
       SUM(recognized_refund_cents) AS recognized_refund_cents,
       SUM(gross_cents - recognized_refund_cents) AS net_cents
FROM per_order
GROUP BY customer_id

title: Find the root, or explain why none exists
prompt: An HR ingestion pipeline cannot assume its reporting hierarchy is a clean tree. For every employee, follow manager links and classify the entire chain. Return employee_id, chain_status, root_employee_id, depth_to_root, issue_node_id ordered by employee_id. The query must terminate without an arbitrary depth limit, including on cycles.
businessRules: employee_id is unique and non-NULL. Each employee has at most one manager_id; NULL means a legitimate root. Multiple separate roots are allowed.
A chain is 'rooted' if it reaches an existing employee whose manager_id is NULL. Return that employee as root_employee_id and the number of manager edges as depth_to_root. A root has depth 0.
A chain is 'orphan' if it points to a manager ID absent from the table. issue_node_id is that missing ID, even for an employee several links below the break.
A chain is 'cycle' if following the next manager would revisit an ID already in this employee's path. issue_node_id is that first repeated ID for this particular starting employee.
For orphan/cycle chains, root_employee_id and depth_to_root are NULL. For rooted chains, issue_node_id is NULL. Return all employees, including those downstream of corrupt links.
Self-reporting is a cycle. Employee names are descriptive only; traverse by ID. No fixed maximum hierarchy depth is guaranteed.

tables.name: h10_employees
tables.description: Unique employee IDs with at most one manager each. The source can contain missing managers and cycles.

setupSql:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS h10_employees;
CREATE TABLE h10_employees (employee_id INTEGER, employee_name VARCHAR, manager_id INTEGER);

(1, 'Ari', NULL),
(2, 'Bo', 1),
(3, 'Cam', 2),
(4, 'Dee', 1),
(5, 'Eli', 99),
(6, 'Flo', 5),

(8, 'Hal', 9),
(9, 'Ira', 7),
(10, 'Jo', 8),
(11, 'Kai', 11),

starterSql:
-- Track a path per starting employee; stop before revisiting a node.
SELECT * FROM h10_employees ORDER BY employee_id;
solutionSql:
WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
  SELECT employee_id AS start_id, employee_id AS current_id, manager_id AS next_id,
         [employee_id] AS path, 0 AS depth
  FROM h10_employees
  UNION ALL
  SELECT w.start_id, m.employee_id, m.manager_id,
         LIST_APPEND(w.path, m.employee_id), w.depth + 1
  FROM walk w
  JOIN h10_employees m ON w.next_id = m.employee_id
  WHERE NOT LIST_CONTAINS(w.path, m.employee_id)
), terminal AS (
  SELECT w.*, m.employee_id AS next_exists
  FROM walk w
  LEFT JOIN h10_employees m ON w.next_id = m.employee_id
  WHERE w.next_id IS NULL
     OR m.employee_id IS NULL
     OR LIST_CONTAINS(w.path, w.next_id)
)
SELECT start_id AS employee_id,
       CASE WHEN next_id IS NULL THEN 'rooted'
            WHEN next_exists IS NULL THEN 'orphan'
            ELSE 'cycle' END AS chain_status,
       CASE WHEN next_id IS NULL THEN current_id ELSE NULL END AS root_employee_id,
       CASE WHEN next_id IS NULL THEN depth ELSE NULL END AS depth_to_root,
       CASE WHEN next_id IS NULL THEN NULL ELSE next_id END AS issue_node_id
FROM terminal
ORDER BY employee_id;
explanation: Seed one upward walk for every employee, not just roots. This preserves employees who belong to disconnected cycles or inherit a broken manager link.

Carry the IDs visited by that starting employee. Before traversing to the manager, verify the next ID is not already in the path. With a finite table and one manager per employee, this guarantees termination without inventing a depth cap.

A terminal row has a NULL next manager, a missing next manager, or a next manager already in its path. Classify those three cases and expose the requested diagnostic ID. Only a real root yields a valid depth.

Join the next manager to the employee table, append the manager ID, and recurse only if that ID is not already in this path.
After recursion, select terminal paths: next_id IS NULL, next manager missing, or LIST_CONTAINS(path, next_id). These map to rooted, orphan, and cycle respectively.
pitfalls: Starting only from roots silently omits cycles and orphans.
Using UNION instead of UNION ALL does not prevent cycles when depth or path changes on every visit.
A hard-coded maximum depth can misclassify a valid deep hierarchy.
A cycle's diagnostic ID depends on the starting employee; it is not necessarily the smallest ID in the cycle.

wrongQueries.label: Traverse downward only from valid roots
wrongQueries.sql:
WITH RECURSIVE rooted AS (
  SELECT employee_id, employee_id AS root_employee_id, 0 AS depth_to_root
  FROM h10_employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.employee_id, r.root_employee_id, r.depth_to_root + 1
  FROM rooted r JOIN h10_employees e ON e.manager_id = r.employee_id
)
SELECT employee_id, 'rooted' AS chain_status, root_employee_id,
       depth_to_root, NULL::INTEGER AS issue_node_id
FROM rooted ORDER BY employee_id;
